cards.front: Recall a key point about Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals
cards.back: Ferrous metals contain iron - magnetic, prone to rust (except stainless). Mild steel: low carbon, ductile, weldable. Stainless steel: chromium content prevents corrosion - cutlery, medical instruments.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals
cards.back: Cast iron: high carbon (2-4%), excellent compressive strength, self-lubricating - engine blocks, manhole covers.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals
cards.back: Aluminium: lightweight (1/3 steel's density), corrosion-resistant (oxide layer), excellent conductor - aircraft, cans, window frames.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals
cards.back: Copper: excellent electrical and thermal conductor, ductile, malleable, antimicrobial - wiring, plumbing, PCBs.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ferrous and Non-Ferrous Metals
cards.back: Brass: copper-zinc alloy - gold appearance, corrosion resistant, low friction, machinable - decorative hardware, valves, musical instruments.

cards.front: What should you know about d&t exam tips?
cards.back: For metal questions: 1) Classify as ferrous/non-ferrous, 2) State key properties with data, 3) Link to product requirements, 4) Consider surface treatments (galvanising, anodising).

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: All metals are magnetic because they are metals. Correct: Only ferrous metals (containing iron) are magnetic - mild steel, cast iron. Non-ferrous metals (aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver) are NOT magnetic. Some stainless steel grades are weakly magnetic due to crystal structure.
A company is designing a lightweight camping stove. Compare aluminium and mild steel for the main body, justifying your recommendation with reference to at least four properties.
